content: A lighter is a compact, portable device designed to produce a flame. It typically consists of a container made of metal or plastic, which holds a flammable liquid such as naphtha or pressurized liquid butane. The device also includes a mechanism for ignition and a method to extinguish the flame, either by cutting off its air supply or fuel source. Lighters that use naphtha contain a wick that is immersed in the liquid fuel, allowing it to become saturated. These lighters often include a fiber packing material that absorbs the liquid to prevent leakage. Additionally, they are equipped with an enclosed top to minimize evaporation of the volatile liquid and to facilitate the extinguishing of the flame. Butane lighters, on the other hand, feature a valved orifice that regulates the release of butane gas. Ignition is achieved either by striking a piece of metal against a flint or by pressing a button that compresses a piezoelectric crystal, generating a spark or voltaic arc. In naphtha lighters, the liquid fuel is sufficiently volatile to release flammable gas as soon as the top is opened. Butane lighters combine the action of striking with the simultaneous opening of the valve to release gas. The spark ignites the gas, producing a flame that persists until the top is closed (in naphtha lighters) or the valve is released (in butane lighters). A metal enclosure with air holes typically surrounds the flame. This design allows for the mixing of fuel and air while reducing the lighter's sensitivity to wind. In butane lighters, the high-energy jet facilitates mixing through Bernoulli's principle, which allows for smaller and more distant air holes compared to other types of lighters. History The first lighter, known as Döbereiner's lamp, was invented by Johann Wolfgang Döbereiner in 1823. Interestingly, the first match was created earlier, in 1805, but the modern friction match (using a phosphorus compound) was not developed until 1827, four years after the invention of the lighter. Lighter Re-Distribution It is a common phenomenon for cigarette lighters to change ownership multiple times during their lifespan. A study conducted at TVU in Reading revealed that an average disposable lighter passes through the hands of seven different smokers before it becomes unusable. Furthermore, only one out of 45 lighters survives until it is completely depleted or non-functional. Car Cigarette Lighters Most automobiles are equipped with an electric cigarette lighter plug that fits into a designated socket. When activated, the internal heating element of the lighter becomes glowing orange-hot within seconds, making it capable of igniting cigarettes, cigars, and even tinder. The lighter socket also doubles as a 12-volt power outlet, which can be used to power various small electrical devices. In newer car models, the lighter plug is often omitted due to the declining popularity of smoking in certain countries and the increasing demand for in-car electronics. However, the socket itself is usually retained as a power source. In Pop Culture At live concerts, particularly during slow songs or power ballads, it has become a tradition for audience members to wave lighters in the air. This practice is gradually being replaced by the waving of mobile phones, both for safety reasons and due to the growing prevalence of mobile phone users compared to smokers. History of the Tradition The origin of waving lighters at concerts is difficult to trace, as it appears to have been influenced by multiple sources. One theory suggests that the practice began at a Neil Diamond concert in 1972 or a Bob Dylan concert in 1974, simply because audience members had lighters available. Another theory posits that the gesture is symbolic of songs referencing flames, such as The Doors' Light My Fire. A further theory links the tradition to a performance at Woodstock, where candles (rather than lighters) were held aloft, and the practice evolved from there.
